title: Optic flow based perception of two-dimensional trajectories and the effects of a single landmark.

findings.antecedent: optic flow stimulus
findings.quote: Yaw was perceived correctly.

findings.antecedent: simulated orientation fixed in space or relative to the trajectory
findings.quote: Perception of the travelled path was less accurate, but still good when the simulated orientation was fixed in space or relative to the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: amount of yaw not equal to or opposite to path rotation
findings.mechanism: yaw was wrongly attributed to a rotation of the path
findings.quote: When the amount of yaw was not equal to the rotation of the path, or in the opposite direction, subjects still perceived orientation as fixed relative to the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: single landmark presence
findings.quote: A single landmark could improve perception.

findings.antecedent: optic flow
findings.quote: Our results indicate that it is possible to reconstruct travelled paths from optic flow.

findings.antecedent: task of reconstructing travelled paths from optic flow
findings.quote: almost all subjects indicated that this was a difficult task.

findings.antecedent: optic flow stimulus
findings.quote: Most indicated that they had experienced impressions of ego-motion (vection).

findings.antecedent: relatively large amount of yaw relative to simulated translation
findings.mechanism: subjects often reproduced a rotation in place
findings.quote: When the stimulus simulated a relatively large amount of yaw relative to the simulated translation, subjects often reproduced a rotation in place.

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark
findings.quote: The presence of a landmark was perceived as helpful, but only in the cases where it was stationary in the field of view ("fixated"); otherwise it was considered a distraction.

findings.antecedent: observer's orientation fixed in space (linear lateral, oblique, semicircle no-turn conditions)
findings.quote: When the observer's orientation is fixed in space (conditions linear lateral or oblique and semicircle no-turn), performance is generally good.

findings.antecedent: observer's orientation fixed only relative to trajectory or not at all
findings.quote: Performance decreases when the orientation is fixed only relative to the trajectory, or not at all.

findings.antecedent: simulated yaw in itself
findings.quote: The apparent difficulty of these stimuli is not caused by the simulated yaw in itself.

findings.antecedent: larger radius of manoeuvre
findings.quote: Performance is generally better at the larger radius.

findings.antecedent: landmark presence (in semicircle inward and no-turn conditions)
findings.quote: In most cases, there is a clear increase in performance when a landmark is present.

findings.antecedent: orientation in space fixed (linear trajectories without yaw)
findings.quote: Subjects can accurately perceive the path-relative orientation when the orientation in space remains fixed (linear trajectories without yaw).

findings.antecedent: curvilinear paths
findings.quote: On curvilinear paths, perception depends on the proportion of simulated rotation vs. translation, and on the simulated orientation relative to the path.

findings.antecedent: large semicircle outward (vs. semicircle forward or inward)
findings.quote: Thus, perception was better for a large semicircle outward (but path rotation, Ψp, was undershot) than for a semicircle forward, that was in turn better than perception for a semicircle inward.

findings.antecedent: small radius of manoeuvre
findings.quote: When the radius was small, there were instead many rotation-in-place responses.

findings.antecedent: simulated yaw (Ψo)
findings.quote: Subjects appear to be capable to approximate the angle over which they are rotated, even during complex manoeuvres (figure 3).

findings.antecedent: linear+yaw stimuli
findings.direction: overshoot for smaller rotations, undershoot for large rotation (Ψo=360°)
findings.quote: A small range effect occurs for the linear+yaw stimuli: overshoot for the smaller rotations, and undershoot for the large rotation (Ψo=360°).

findings.antecedent: stimulus does not simulate any observer rotation
findings.quote: Yaw is never perceived when the stimulus does not simulate any observer rotation (also cf. Bertin et al. 2000).

findings.antecedent: simulated manoeuvre
findings.quote: Our results show that subjects could perceive the qualitative nature of a simulated manoeuvre; correct directions, the correct form of trajectory and sometimes also the correct average orientation relative to the trajectory (<Фr>).

findings.antecedent: optic flow
findings.quote: Our results suggest that subjects could indeed correctly detect the angle (Ψo) over which they were turned.

findings.antecedent: simulated trajectory linear
findings.quote: The reconstruction of the travelled trajectory was correct when the simulated trajectory was linear.

findings.antecedent: orientation yoked to path and tangential to trajectory
findings.quote: Subjects were indeed capable of correctly judging the rotation of the path when orientation was yoked to the path, but only when it was tangential to the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: orientation inward or outward (relative to center of rotation)
findings.mechanism: causing unreliable perception; perceived as rotations in place or as lateral translations
findings.quote: Perception was much less veridical when the orientation was either inward (towards the centre of rotation, causing unreliable perception; perceived as rotations in place) or outward (away from the centre of rotation; perceived as rotations in place or as lateral translations when the radius was large).

findings.antecedent: yaw in same direction as path rotation and increased
findings.quote: When yaw (in the same direction as the path rotation) increased, perception became less veridical (path rotation was undershot), until there was more than half as much yaw as path rotation.

findings.antecedent: simulated path
findings.mechanism: may be in line with the results from a recent study by van den Berg et al. (2001) who found that subjects tend to undershoot the curvature of the simulated path.
findings.quote: The average reported path rotation was always less than the presented value for the stimuli discussed above, even if the difference was not always significant.

findings.antecedent: yaw in direction opposite to path rotation
findings.mechanism: a semicircle could be perceived as a straight line, or as a curvilinear manoeuvre in the opposite direction
findings.quote: Surprisingly, the attribution also occurred for the stimuli in which yaw was in the direction opposite to the path rotation.

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark
findings.quote: In general, the subjects reported that the presence of a landmark facilitated the task, but only when it remained stationary in the field of view.

findings.antecedent: landmark presence
findings.consequent: resemblance of reproductions to actual manoeuvres (figural distance)
findings.quote: This was confirmed by the figural distance measure: the reproductions indeed resembled the actually presented manoeuvres more when a landmark was present than when it was absent.

findings.antecedent: landmark presence in linear+yaw conditions
findings.consequent: veridicality of path rotation and yaw perception
findings.quote: For the linear+yaw conditions, perception of path rotation and yaw was more veridical when a landmark was present.

findings.antecedent: landmark presence * proportion of simulated yaw (more yaw in short trajectory version)
findings.quote: we found that the perception of path rotation benefited more from the presence of a landmark when the simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally more yaw (that is, more in the short trajectory version than in the long version).

findings.antecedent: landmark presence * proportion of simulated yaw (less yaw in long trajectory version)
findings.quote: Perception of yaw improved more due to a landmark when the simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally less yaw (that is, more in the long version than in the short version).

findings.antecedent: landmark presence in some curvilinear conditions
findings.quote: Perception also improved in some of curvilinear conditions.

findings.antecedent: landmark presence (vs. no landmark)
findings.consequent: responses excluded from analysis (for semicircle inward conditions)
findings.quote: Much less responses to the conditions semicircle inward were excluded from analysis when the stimulus contained a landmark that only served as a reference for the movement of the other points, compared to when there was no landmark.

findings.antecedent: landmark presence
findings.quote: There were also less erroneous rotation in place responses when a landmark was present.

findings.antecedent: adding a landmark in majority of curvilinear conditions
findings.mechanism: either the additional information was of no use to the subject, or that the attention needed to interpret that information actually interfered with the ego-motion perception.
findings.quote: In the majority of these conditions, however, there was little effect of adding a landmark, and sometimes even a negative effect.

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark (vs. non-shifting) in linear+yaw conditions
findings.quote: Yet we have some tentative evidence for these conditions that the improvement of path rotation perception was bigger for a shifting landmark than for a non-shifting landmark.

findings.antecedent: simulated 64° yaw against 180° path-rotation in other direction
findings.mechanism: suggests that the accuracy of rotation perception that we found was not solely due to a rough 90° categorisation.
findings.quote: For stimuli simulating 64° yaw against 180° path-rotation in the other direction, the reported path rotation was around 130°. This was not significantly different from 180°-64°=116°

stimuli.description: Optic flow stimuli consisting of dotscapes of white dots (4 pixel diameter; 4800 dots total) on a 50x50m ground surface 1m below virtual eye-level, horizon at 15m. Simulated linear or curvilinear 2D trajectories over a horizontal ground plane. Some stimuli included a single landmark (red dot attached to ground via string of blue dots).

tables.description: Lists stimulus conditions, their descriptions, size (length/radius in meters), and which experiment they were presented in, including landmark type.

Summary of results including globally correct responses, trajectory correct responses, reported rotations in place, total number of responses (N), and number of quantitatively analysed responses (N*) per condition.

limitations: The recorded reproductions that subjects made do not always exactly match how they verbally described them, making it difficult to ascertain if the reproduction corresponded to the actual perception or verbal categorization.
